chapter: South America and back in New York
title: Showmen replace musicians as bandleaders
summary: He says leaders like Cab Calloway, Noble Sissle, Baron Lee and Lucky Millinder were showmen, so people heard with their eyes.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: And then, band conductors got obsolete -- musician band conductors. Because the fad comes in with Cab Calloway, Noble Sisle, and Sunshine Sammy and -- what was this fellow's name --
Baron Lee, and all these fellows. They began to take clowns and stand them in front of the band, you know what I mean?

Performing. And those dancers and things like that.

So, outside of Duke, because he was well established, in front of the band. In fact he played less and less, he too. But that's what happened, was because they wanted showmen in front of the band.

Yeah, yeah. Willy Bryant. And Lucky Millinder. They all, Lucky Millinder would jump up on top of the piano and on top of tables and all like that. Well, that wasn't music. But it worked on the people's eyes. People begin to hear with their eyes. Not with their ears, see?

And it's like, well today, we have a lot of the hard Rocks. They dress outlandish. You see, because that all makes the picture. Because the people are not really -- have time. And when the singers don't enunciate nothing. You don't understand nothing and it's like we were back in the primitive days, you see.
